scalesUsed.notes: A - B - C# - D - E - F# - G# - A
scalesUsed.application: The primary harmonic framework, though the simplicity of the song keeps the melody pentatonic
Vocal melody and guitar riff notes draw from this simpler scale

keyAndScale.modalCharacter: Straightforward major tonality with a I-IV-v progression giving a slightly raw, garage quality
keyAndScale.relativeMinor: F# minor is the relative minor of A major

mainProgression.description: The iconic three-chord riff that loops throughout the entire song. The minor v chord (Em) gives it a slightly unexpected, raw quality compared to a standard I-IV-V.

sectionProgressions.description: The endlessly repeating riff pattern that forms both the verse and chorus. Each chord gets two beats in the pattern.
The same chord progression continues under the famously sloppy, energetic guitar solo.

harmonicFunction: A (I) - Tonic chord providing the major-key home base
D (IV) - Subdominant chord creating the characteristic rising motion from A
Em (v) - Minor dominant adding a raw, garage rock edge to the progression

techniques.name: The Louie Louie Riff
techniques.description: The most famous three-chord riff in rock history, a repeating A-D-Em-D pattern that can be played with open chords or power chords

notes: A: X-0-2-2-2-0 (open A major) or A5: X-0-2-2-X-X (power chord)
D: X-X-0-2-3-2 (open D major) or D5: X-5-7-7-X-X (power chord)
Em: 0-2-2-0-0-0 (open E minor) or E5: 0-2-2-X-X-X (power chord)
The rhythm follows a distinctive da-da-da, da-da pattern on each chord
The riff repeats identically for the entire song with no variation
sequence: Learn A, D, and Em open chord shapes
Practice the riff pattern: A (2 beats) - D (2 beats) - Em (2 beats) - D (2 beats)
Add the signature rhythm: strum on beat 1, skip beat 2, strum-strum on the 'and' of 2 and beat 3
Loop the riff continuously without stopping
tips: The rhythm is more important than clean chord voicings in this song
Listen to the original recording to learn the distinctive strum pattern
Power chord versions (A5, D5, E5) are even easier and sound authentic
Keep it loose and fun - this is not a song about precision

techniques.name: Power Chord Version
techniques.description: Playing the Louie Louie riff using power chords instead of open chords, which simplifies the left hand and adds a heavier, more aggressive tone

notes: A5: 5-7-7-X-X-X (5th fret barre on low E string)
D5: X-5-7-7-X-X (5th fret on A string)
E5: 0-2-2-X-X-X (open power chord)
Power chords use only two or three strings, making transitions faster
The same rhythm pattern applies to the power chord version
sequence: Learn the A5 power chord shape at the 5th fret
Slide down to D5 on the A string at the 5th fret
Drop to the open E5 power chord
Practice transitioning between the three shapes with the song rhythm
tips: Mute unused strings with your fretting hand to avoid unwanted noise
Use palm muting on the bridge for a tighter, punchier sound
The power chord version is great for playing with distortion
This is the version most punk and garage bands use

sections.name: Intro
sections.description: The iconic riff kicks in immediately, establishing the groove that will drive the entire song
notes: The riff starts immediately with no count-in
Establish the groove from the very first strum
The same riff pattern will repeat for the entire song
Lock in with the rhythm section right away

sections.name: Verse
sections.description: The verse uses the same repeating riff under the famously garbled, barely intelligible vocals
notes: Identical riff pattern continues through the verse
The guitar part does not change between sections
Focus on keeping the rhythm steady and the groove locked
The vocal melody rides on top of the unvarying riff

sections.name: Guitar Solo
sections.description: The infamously loose, energetic guitar solo played over the same three-chord riff pattern
notes: For beginners, simply keep strumming the riff during the solo section
The original solo is famously imperfect - do not worry about precision
The chord progression remains identical under the solo
Advanced players can improvise using A major pentatonic over the riff

sections.name: Final Verse / Outro
sections.description: Final verse repetitions and the outro, maintaining the same riff to the very end
notes: Same riff continues unbroken through the final verses
Energy builds slightly toward the ending
The song ends with a final A chord resolution
Maintain steady rhythm right to the last note

guitar.recommended: Any electric guitar with single-coil pickups
alternatives: Acoustic guitar works fine for practice
guitar.pickup: Bridge or middle pickup for a bright, cutting tone

amp.recommended: Fender Bassman or similar tube amp cranked for natural overdrive

effects.distortion: Light overdrive from amp or mild overdrive pedal
effects.other: No effects pedals needed. The lo-fi, raw tone is part of the charm.

beginner.focus: Learn the three chords and the basic riff pattern
steps: Learn open A, D, and Em chord shapes
Practice switching between all three chords smoothly
Learn the riff rhythm: A - D - Em - D with two beats per chord
Loop the riff continuously at a slow tempo

intermediate.focus: Play the full song at tempo with the authentic rhythm feel
steps: Build up to 120 BPM with the riff pattern
Add the signature strum pattern for each chord
Play through the entire song structure without stopping
Practice with the original recording as a backing track

advanced.focus: Add power chords, sing along, and improvise over the riff
steps: Learn the power chord version (A5-D5-E5) for heavier performances
Sing while strumming the riff pattern
Improvise a solo using A major pentatonic during the solo section
Perform with a band or backing track at full energy

commonMistakes: Making it too complicated - this song is supposed to be dead simple
Losing the groove when switching to the Em chord
Playing too cleanly and precisely - embrace the loose, garage feel
Speeding up or slowing down during the repetitive riff
practiceRoutine: Warm up with A, D, Em chord switches for 2 minutes
Practice the riff pattern at 80 BPM for 3 minutes
Increase tempo to 100 BPM and play 3 full cycles
Play at full 120 BPM for several minutes without stopping
Run through the entire song with the recording
focusAreas: Steady tempo without rushing or dragging
Clean chord transitions within the riff
Endurance for playing the same riff for the entire song
metronomeWork: Start at 80 BPM and play 8 cycles of the riff without stopping
Increase by 10 BPM increments up to 120 BPM
Practice at 120 BPM for 3 minutes straight for endurance
Try playing with the metronome on beats 2 and 4 for a natural feel
